                // instantly close" instead of staying open: this window is shown from inside
                // ControllerPollTimer_Tick's WM_TIMER handling rather than from a genuine
                // mouse/keyboard input message, and Windows' foreground-lock heuristic can
                // respond to that by not truly handing it activation - the picker appears on
                // screen but the main window silently stays the real foreground window, which
                // fires Deactivate on THIS form within the same message cycle it was created
                // in, before the user ever did anything.
                //
                // A single BeginInvoke hop (the previous attempt at a fix) turned out not to be
                // enough: SetForegroundWindow fighting the foreground-lock timeout is a real,
                // sometimes multi-hundred-millisecond OS-level negotiation, and by the time the
                // next queued message runs, Windows can still be mid-negotiation with
                // Form.ActiveForm not yet settled back onto this window - so the deferred check
                // saw "not active" and cancelled anyway, which is exactly the flash the person
                // kept seeing. deactivateGuard below is a short arming window instead of a
                // single hop: any Deactivate that fires before it elapses is treated as pure
                // startup noise and ignored outright, and only a Deactivate that happens after
                // the picker has had a moment to genuinely settle is trusted to mean the user
                // actually clicked away.
                //
                // "Clicked away" was also too broad in a second way: Form.ActiveForm becomes
                // null the instant focus leaves this whole application - alt-tabbing to another
                // program, clicking its taskbar icon, a notification stealing focus, even just
                // switching to a browser tab in another window - and that was being treated
                // exactly like clicking the main ModManager window itself, closing this popup
                // either way. Only the latter is what should dismiss it: switching away to
                // something outside the app should leave it exactly as it was, so it's still
                // sitting open (over whichever category/field it belonged to) when the person
                // switches back. Form.ActiveForm is null precisely in that "left the app
                // entirely" case (it only ever reports a form belonging to THIS application),
                // so the check below leaves the picker alone whenever that's what happened and
                // only closes it when some other form of ours - the main window - is what
                // actually took focus.
                Deactivate += delegate
                {
                    if (DialogResult != DialogResult.None) return;
                    if (!deactivateGuardArmed) return;
                    BeginInvoke(new MethodInvoker(delegate
                    {
                        if (DialogResult != DialogResult.None || ReferenceEquals(Form.ActiveForm, this) || ContainsFocus) return;
                        if (Form.ActiveForm == null) return;
                        // Fix: Y/BeginTyping opens the on-screen keyboard OWNED by this same
                        // picker (see ShowVirtualKeyboard - target.FindForm() resolves to this
                        // picker while typing into its search row), and that hand-off of real
                        // Windows focus to the keyboard fires this exact Deactivate. Without this
                        // check the picker treated its own keyboard grabbing focus exactly like
                        // the main window stealing it and cancelled itself out from under it -
                        // intermittently, depending on whether the 350ms guard above had already
                        // armed by the time the keyboard finished activating, which is why Y only
                        // "stuck" every several tries instead of every time.
                        if (Host != null && ReferenceEquals(Form.ActiveForm, Host.frmVirtualKeyboard)) return;
                        CancelPicker();
                    }));
                };

                // See the Deactivate comment above - this is the first line of defense against
                // the same race, forcing this window to genuinely take OS foreground
                // activation instead of relying on ShowDialog to have already secured it.
                // deactivateGuardTimer arms the Deactivate handler above only once the window
                // has had a brief moment (see DeactivateGuardDelayMs) to finish that
                // negotiation, instead of trusting the very first Deactivate it receives.
                Shown += delegate
                {
                    SetForegroundWindow(Handle);
                    Activate();
                    ClampToScreen();
                    deactivateGuardTimer = new Timer { Interval = DeactivateGuardDelayMs };
                    deactivateGuardTimer.Tick += delegate
                    {
                        deactivateGuardArmed = true;
                        deactivateGuardTimer.Stop();
                        deactivateGuardTimer.Dispose();
                        deactivateGuardTimer = null;
                    };
                    deactivateGuardTimer.Start();
                };

                FormClosed += delegate
                {
                    if (deactivateGuardTimer != null)
                    {
                        deactivateGuardTimer.Stop();
                        deactivateGuardTimer.Dispose();
                        deactivateGuardTimer = null;
                    }
                };

                Load += delegate
                {
                    // Deferred until the box is parented and realised: AttachSearchIcon sets
                    // the edit control's left margin through a window message, which is lost
                    // if the handle is recreated afterwards by re-parenting.
                    if (SearchEnabled) Host.AttachSearchIcon(txtSearch);
                    LayoutPicker();
                    RefreshHighlight();
                };

                LayoutPicker();
                ApplyQuery();
                SelectInitialValue();

                ShowDialog(host);
            }

            // Second half of the off-screen fix started at the ClientSize clamp in
            // BuildAndShow: CenterParent centers this window on the HOST window, not the
            // screen, so a host sitting near a screen edge (or spanning a second monitor) can
            // still leave part of this borderless popup - buttons included - past the visible
            // working area even with a screen-aware size. Nudges the window back inside the
            // current monitor's working area as the last step before the person can interact
            // with it, the same way Windows itself keeps a dialog from opening off-screen.
            private void ClampToScreen()
            {
                Rectangle workArea = Screen.FromControl(this).WorkingArea;
                int x = Location.X;
                int y = Location.Y;
                if (x + Width > workArea.Right) x = workArea.Right - Width;
                if (y + Height > workArea.Bottom) y = workArea.Bottom - Height;
                if (x < workArea.Left) x = workArea.Left;
                if (y < workArea.Top) y = workArea.Top;
                Location = new Point(x, y);
            }

            private void SelectInitialValue()
            {
                if (!string.IsNullOrEmpty(InitialValue))
                {
                    int idx = items.IndexOf(InitialValue);
                    if (idx >= 0) selIndex = idx;
                }
                // With nothing to land on, start on the search row instead of highlighting a
                // grid that has no tiles in it.
                if (tiles.Count == 0 && SearchEnabled) searchRowFocused = true;
                RefreshHighlight();
            }

            private void LayoutPicker()
            {
                const int border = 2;
                const int footerHeight = 36;
                const int titleBarHeight = 44;
                const int backButtonWidth = 90;
                const int backGap = 6;

                int w = ClientSize.Width;
                int h = ClientSize.Height;
                int y = border;

                btnBack.Bounds = new Rectangle(border, y, backButtonWidth, titleBarHeight);
                lblTitle.Bounds = new Rectangle(border + backButtonWidth + backGap, y,
                    w - border * 2 - backButtonWidth - backGap, titleBarHeight);
                y += titleBarHeight;

                if (SearchEnabled)
                {
                    txtSearch.Location = new Point(12, 10);
                    txtSearch.Width = Math.Max(80, w - border * 2 - 24);
                    // A single-line TextBox sizes its own height from its font, so the row is
                    // measured from the box rather than the other way round.
                    int rowHeight = txtSearch.Height + 20;
                    pnlSearchRow.Bounds = new Rectangle(border, y, w - border * 2, rowHeight);
                    lblPlaceholder.Bounds = new Rectangle(22, 0, Math.Max(10, txtSearch.ClientSize.Width - 24), txtSearch.ClientSize.Height);
                    y += rowHeight;
                }

                pnlResults.Bounds = new Rectangle(border, y, w - border * 2, Math.Max(60, h - y - footerHeight - border));
                btnFooterBack.Bounds = new Rectangle(border, h - footerHeight - border, w - border * 2, footerHeight);

                LayoutTiles();
            }

            private void ApplyQuery()
            {
                CurrentQuery = (txtSearch != null) ? txtSearch.Text : "";
                if (lblPlaceholder != null) lblPlaceholder.Visible = (CurrentQuery.Length == 0);

                List<string> supplied = (ItemProvider != null) ? ItemProvider(CurrentQuery) : null;
                items.Clear();
                if (supplied != null) items.AddRange(supplied);

                RebuildTiles();
            }

            private void RebuildTiles()
            {
                for (int i = 0; i < tiles.Count; i++)
                {
                    pnlResults.Controls.Remove(tiles[i]);
                    tiles[i].Dispose();
                }
                tiles.Clear();

                // Narrow the grid for short lists so four themes do not end up as three tiles
                // and a gap, and a single match fills the row it is on. Also forced to a
                // single column whenever any entry's label is long - the Console Mode
                // Settings menu's "Console Mode (Steam Deck):  ON/OFF" style entries were
                // getting squeezed into a 2-column grid (four entries) narrow enough that
                // the label (and critically, the ON/OFF it ends with) was cut off at the
                // tile's edge instead of getting the full window width to lay out in.
                bool anyLongLabel = false;
                for (int li = 0; li < items.Count; li++)
                {
                    if (items[li] != null && items[li].Length > 26) { anyLongLabel = true; break; }
                }
                columns = anyLongLabel ? 1 : ((items.Count <= 1) ? 1 : ((items.Count <= 4) ? 2 : 3));

                for (int i = 0; i < items.Count; i++)
                {
                    int captured = i;
                    ShinyButton tile = new ShinyButton
                    {
                        Text = items[i],
                        Font = new Font(FontFamily.GenericSansSerif, 10f, FontStyle.Bold),
                        FlatStyle = FlatStyle.Flat,
                        BackColor = theme.ButtonBg,
                        ForeColor = theme.ButtonFg
                    };
                    tile.Click += delegate { selIndex = captured; searchRowFocused = false; ActivateSelection(); };
                    tile.MouseEnter += delegate { selIndex = captured; searchRowFocused = false; RefreshHighlight(); };
                    tiles.Add(tile);
                    pnlResults.Controls.Add(tile);
                }

                if (selIndex > tiles.Count - 1) selIndex = Math.Max(0, tiles.Count - 1);
                lblEmpty.Visible = (tiles.Count == 0);

                // LayoutTiles positions tiles in unscrolled coordinates, so the panel has to be
                // back at the top before it runs or a scrolled-down grid would be rebuilt
                // underneath a stale scroll offset and appear to jump.
                pnlResults.AutoScrollPosition = new Point(0, 0);
                LayoutTiles();
                RefreshHighlight();
            }

            private void LayoutTiles()
            {
                const int gap = 10;
                const int pad = 12;
                // A single-column grid only happens for short lists or long labels (see
                // RebuildTiles) - either way there's room to spare, so long labels get a
                // taller tile to wrap into instead of squeezing a second line into the same
                // 74px a short one-line tile uses.
                int tileHeight = (columns == 1) ? 88 : 74;

                // Reserve the scrollbar's width up front so the grid does not re-wrap the
                // instant the list grows long enough for one to appear.
                int avail = pnlResults.ClientSize.Width - pad * 2 - 18;
                if (avail < 140) avail = 140;

                lblEmpty.Bounds = new Rectangle(pad, pad + 16, avail, 40);

                if (tiles.Count == 0) return;

                int cols = Math.Max(1, columns);
                int tileWidth = (avail - gap * (cols - 1)) / cols;
                if (tileWidth < 80) tileWidth = 80;

                for (int i = 0; i < tiles.Count; i++)
                {
                    int r = i / cols;
                    int c = i % cols;
                    tiles[i].Location = new Point(pad + c * (tileWidth + gap), pad + r * (tileHeight + gap));
                    tiles[i].Size = new Size(tileWidth, tileHeight);
                }
            }

            private void RefreshHighlight()
            {
                for (int i = 0; i < tiles.Count; i++)
                {
                    bool sel = (!searchRowFocused && i == selIndex);
                    tiles[i].BackColor = sel ? theme.AccentColor : theme.ButtonBg;
                    tiles[i].ForeColor = sel ? Color.White : theme.ButtonFg;
                }

                if (SearchEnabled && pnlSearchRow != null)
                {
                    pnlSearchRow.BackColor = searchRowFocused ? BlendColors(theme.AccentColor, theme.WindowBg, 0.55f) : theme.WindowBg;
                }

                if (!searchRowFocused && selIndex >= 0 && selIndex < tiles.Count)
                {
                    ShinyButton tile = tiles[selIndex];
                    pnlRing.Bounds = new Rectangle(tile.Left - 4, tile.Top - 4, tile.Width + 8, tile.Height + 8);
                    pnlRing.Visible = true;
                    pnlRing.SendToBack();
                    pnlRing.Invalidate();
                    // Only once the panel is real - the first ApplyQuery runs before
                    // ShowDialog, when there is nothing on screen to scroll yet.
                    if (pnlResults.IsHandleCreated) pnlResults.ScrollControlIntoView(tile);
                }
                else
                {
                    pnlRing.Visible = false;
                }

                btnFooterBack.Text = SearchEnabled
                    ? "\u2195 \u2194 Navigate     (A) Select     (Y) Type     (B) / Click Back"
                    : "\u2195 \u2194 Navigate     (A) Select     (B) / Click Back";
            }

            // Called by the host's poll timer for every direction, whatever the input source.
            public void MoveSelection(bool up, bool down, bool left, bool right)
            {
                if (searchRowFocused)
                {
                    // Down off the search row drops straight into the first result, which is
                    // the one thing the row's own hint promises.
                    if (down && tiles.Count > 0)
                    {
                        searchRowFocused = false;
                        selIndex = 0;
                        // Hand real focus off the box as well, so keystrokes stop landing in a
                        // query the cursor has visibly left.
                        ActiveControl = null;
                        RefreshHighlight();
                    }
                    return;
                }

                if (tiles.Count == 0)
                {
                    if (up && SearchEnabled) { searchRowFocused = true; RefreshHighlight(); }
                    return;
                }

                int next = selIndex;
                if (up) next -= columns;
                if (down) next += columns;
                if (left) next -= 1;
                if (right) next += 1;

                if (next < 0)
                {
                    // Off the top of the grid is the search row, when there is one.
                    if (up && SearchEnabled) { searchRowFocused = true; RefreshHighlight(); return; }
                    next = 0;
                }

                if (next > tiles.Count - 1)
                {
                    // Down from a full row into a short last row still lands on the last
                    // result rather than refusing to move at all.
                    next = (down && selIndex < tiles.Count - 1) ? tiles.Count - 1 : selIndex;
                }

                if (next != selIndex)
                {
                    selIndex = next;
                    RefreshHighlight();
                }
            }

            public void ActivateSelection()
            {
                if (searchRowFocused) { BeginTyping(); return; }
                if (selIndex < 0 || selIndex >= items.Count) return;

                SelectedValue = items[selIndex];
                CloseKeyboardIfOpen();
                DialogResult = DialogResult.OK;
                Close();
            }

            // Repainted by the host's pulse timer so the picker's outline breathes in step
            // with every other ring in the app.
            public void PulseRing()
            {
                if (pnlRing != null && pnlRing.Visible) pnlRing.Invalidate();
            }

            public void CancelPicker()
            {
                SelectedValue = null;
                CloseKeyboardIfOpen();
                DialogResult = DialogResult.Cancel;
                Close();
            }

            // The (Y TO TYPE) shortcut: park on the search row and summon the on-screen
            // keyboard for it, which is the only way a controller-only session can type at all.
            public void BeginTyping()
            {
                if (!SearchEnabled || txtSearch == null) return;

                searchRowFocused = true;
                RefreshHighlight();
                txtSearch.Focus();
                Host.ShowVirtualKeyboard(txtSearch);
            }

            private void CloseKeyboardIfOpen()
            {
                if (Host != null && Host.frmVirtualKeyboard != null && Host.frmVirtualKeyboard.Visible)
                {
                    Host.HideVirtualKeyboard();
                }
            }

            // Same mechanism the main window and the virtual keyboard use (see the comment on
            // VirtualKeyboardForm): arrow keys only mark a direction physically held, and the
            // host's poll timer performs the move, so a held arrow key and a held D-pad
            // direction repeat at exactly the same speed here as everywhere else.
            protected override bool ProcessCmdKey(ref Message msg, Keys keyData)
            {
                bool typing = (txtSearch != null && txtSearch.Focused);

                if (keyData == Keys.Escape) { CancelPicker(); return true; }
                if (keyData == Keys.Enter) { ActivateSelection(); return true; }
                if (keyData == Keys.Tab || keyData == (Keys.Tab | Keys.Shift)) return true;

                // While the caret is genuinely in the search box, Left/Right belong to the
                // caret and Space belongs to the query.
                if (typing && (keyData == Keys.Left || keyData == Keys.Right || keyData == Keys.Space))
                {
                    return base.ProcessCmdKey(ref msg, keyData);
                }

                if (Host != null)
                {
                    if (keyData == Keys.Up) { Host.physUpHeld = true; return true; }
                    if (keyData == Keys.Down) { Host.physDownHeld = true; return true; }
                    if (keyData == Keys.Left) { Host.physLeftHeld = true; return true; }
                    if (keyData == Keys.Right) { Host.physRightHeld = true; return true; }
                }

                if (keyData == Keys.Space) { ActivateSelection(); return true; }

                return base.ProcessCmdKey(ref msg, keyData);
            }

            protected override void OnPaint(PaintEventArgs e)
            {
                base.OnPaint(e);
                if (theme == null) return;

                // Borderless, so this accent frame is the only thing separating the picker
                // from the window behind it.
                using (Pen pen = new Pen(theme.AccentColor, 2f))
                {
                    e.Graphics.DrawRectangle(pen, 1, 1, ClientSize.Width - 2, ClientSize.Height - 2);
                }
            }
        }

        private void OnConsoleModeChanged(object sender, EventArgs e)
        {
            bool consoleOn = chkConsoleMode.Checked;
            pnlConsoleTiles.Visible = consoleOn;
            ApplyConsoleTopBarLayout(consoleOn);

            if (consoleOn)
            {
                pnlConsoleTiles.BringToFront();
                selectedConsoleCategoryIndex = 0;
                selectedConsoleTileIndex = 0;
                consoleLaunchFocused = false;
                consoleResizeFocused = false;
                listResizeModeActive = false;
                consoleTopBarActive = false;
                consoleSidebarFocused = false;
                consoleSidebarIndex = 0;
                consoleDropdownOpen = false;
                RebuildConsoleCategoryContent();
                RefreshConsoleHighlights();
                pnlConsoleTiles.Focus();
                controllerPollTimer.Start();
            }
            else
            {
                listResizeModeActive = false;
                consoleTopBarActive = false;
                consoleSidebarFocused = false;
                consoleResizeFocused = false;
                if (consoleDropdownOpen) CloseConsoleDropdown(true);
                if (pnlTopBarFocusHighlight != null) pnlTopBarFocusHighlight.Visible = false;

                // The keyboard can still be legitimately open on its own (a controller user
                // summoned it without Console Mode ever being on) - only stop the poll timer
                // if it isn't.
                if (frmVirtualKeyboard == null || !frmVirtualKeyboard.Visible)
                {
                    controllerPollTimer.Stop();
                }
            }

            SaveCheckboxSettings();
        }

        // Performs one directional move in whichever navigation context is currently active -
        // shared by the edge-triggered first press AND the hold-to-repeat timer below, so the
        // two can never drift out of sync with each other or with what a single press does.
        private void FireDirectionalMove(bool up, bool down, bool left, bool right)
        {
            if (!up && !down && !left && !right) return;

            bool keyboardVisible = frmVirtualKeyboard != null && frmVirtualKeyboard.Visible;
            if (keyboardVisible)
            {
                if (up) MoveKeyboardSelection(-1, 0);
                if (down) MoveKeyboardSelection(1, 0);
                if (left) MoveKeyboardSelection(0, -1);
                if (right) MoveKeyboardSelection(0, 1);
            }
            else if (activeConsolePicker != null)
            {
                // A picker is modal, so this timer is ticking inside its nested message loop
                // and it owns every direction until it closes.
                activeConsolePicker.MoveSelection(up, down, left, right);
            }
            else if (consoleDropdownOpen)
            {
                // While the list is actually open, Up/Down walk it and Left/Right are ignored -
                // nudging the value sideways underneath an open list would be incoherent.
                if (up) MoveConsoleDropdownSelection(-1);
                if (down) MoveConsoleDropdownSelection(1);
            }
            else if (consoleTopBarActive)
            {
                if (up) MoveConsoleTopBarSelection(-1);
                if (down) MoveConsoleTopBarSelection(1);
                if (left) AdjustConsoleTopBarValue(-1);
                if (right) AdjustConsoleTopBarValue(1);
            }
            else if (listResizeModeActive)
            {
                // Down grows the list, Up shrinks it - see the matching comment on the
                // desktop-keyboard branch in ProcessCmdKey for why this direction was flipped.
                if (down) AdjustServerListHeight(lstServerPaks.Height + 20);
                if (up) AdjustServerListHeight(lstServerPaks.Height - 20);
            }
            else if (consoleSidebarFocused)
            {
                if (up) MoveConsoleSidebarSelection(-1);
                if (down) MoveConsoleSidebarSelection(1);
                if (right) LeaveConsoleSidebar();
                // Left is a no-op here: the sidebar is already the leftmost zone.
            }
            else
            {
                if (up) MoveConsoleTileSelection(-1);
                if (down) MoveConsoleTileSelection(1);
                // Left moves focus to the sidebar instead of switching category outright;
                // Right is a no-op because the content tiles are the rightmost zone.
                if (left) EnterConsoleSidebar();
            }
        }

        // Advances one direction's hold timer by one poll interval and returns true the
        // instant it should fire another move: once when it first crosses
        // RepeatInitialDelayMs, then again every RepeatIntervalMs after that for as long as
        // "held" stays true. Resets cleanly the moment the direction is released, so the next
        // press always starts with the same initial delay rather than repeating immediately.
        private bool AdvanceRepeat(bool held, ref int heldMs, ref bool repeating)
        {
            if (!held)
            {
                heldMs = 0;
                repeating = false;
                return false;
            }

            heldMs += controllerPollTimer.Interval;

            if (!repeating)
            {
                if (heldMs < RepeatInitialDelayMs) return false;
                repeating = true;
                heldMs -= RepeatInitialDelayMs;
                return true;
            }

            if (heldMs < RepeatIntervalMs) return false;
            heldMs -= RepeatIntervalMs;
            return true;
        }

        private void ControllerPollTimer_Tick(object sender, EventArgs e)
        {
            bool keyboardVisible = frmVirtualKeyboard != null && frmVirtualKeyboard.Visible;

            // The poll timer now has three independent reasons to be running: Console Mode
            // itself, the virtual keyboard (which a controller user can summon without ever
            // turning Console Mode on), and hold-to-repeat for a physically-held arrow key
            // (physUpHeld etc.) - which can only be true while one of the other two is also
            // true, since that's the only time ProcessCmdKey/frmVirtualKeyboard's KeyDown set
            // them, so this guard still covers all three.
            if ((chkConsoleMode == null || !chkConsoleMode.Checked) && !keyboardVisible) return;

            // A System.Windows.Forms.Timer keeps firing even while a modal dialog (like
            // Settings) is showing on top, since it isn't tied to window focus at all - without
            // this check, pressing A on a controller while some other dialog is open would
            // also silently activate whatever console tile is behind it. The keyboard is its
            // own owned Form, so it also counts as a valid "active" target while it's shown.
            bool activeIsRelevant = ReferenceEquals(Form.ActiveForm, this)
                || (keyboardVisible && ReferenceEquals(Form.ActiveForm, frmVirtualKeyboard))
                || (activeConsolePicker != null && ReferenceEquals(Form.ActiveForm, activeConsolePicker));
            if (!activeIsRelevant) return;

            // Unlike before, a missing/disconnected controller no longer bails out of the
            // whole tick - a physically-held arrow key still needs this same timer to drive
            // its hold-to-repeat below, whether or not a controller is even plugged in.
            XINPUT_STATE state;
            bool haveController = TryGetControllerState(out state);

            ushort buttons = haveController ? state.Gamepad.wButtons : (ushort)0;
            bool dpadUp = haveController && (buttons & XINPUT_GAMEPAD_DPAD_UP) != 0;
            bool dpadDown = haveController && (buttons & XINPUT_GAMEPAD_DPAD_DOWN) != 0;
            bool dpadLeft = haveController && (buttons & XINPUT_GAMEPAD_DPAD_LEFT) != 0;
            bool dpadRight = haveController && (buttons & XINPUT_GAMEPAD_DPAD_RIGHT) != 0;
            bool aButton = haveController && (buttons & XINPUT_GAMEPAD_A) != 0;
            bool bButton = haveController && (buttons & XINPUT_GAMEPAD_B) != 0;
            bool yButton = haveController && (buttons & XINPUT_GAMEPAD_Y) != 0;
            bool prevAButton = (prevControllerButtons & XINPUT_GAMEPAD_A) != 0;
            bool prevBButton = (prevControllerButtons & XINPUT_GAMEPAD_B) != 0;
            bool prevYButton = (prevControllerButtons & XINPUT_GAMEPAD_Y) != 0;

            // The left stick works as a D-pad substitute too - some controllers (and Steam
            // Input's default desktop-mode mapping on Steam Deck) report movement there
            // instead of on the D-pad bits.
            bool stickUp = haveController && state.Gamepad.sThumbLY > XINPUT_STICK_THRESHOLD;
            bool stickDown = haveController && state.Gamepad.sThumbLY < -XINPUT_STICK_THRESHOLD;
            bool stickLeft = haveController && state.Gamepad.sThumbLX < -XINPUT_STICK_THRESHOLD;
            bool stickRight = haveController && state.Gamepad.sThumbLX > XINPUT_STICK_THRESHOLD;

            // Combined "is this direction being pushed right now" from every source at once -
            // D-pad, left stick, or a physically-held arrow key. Both the instant first move
            // (the rising edge against last tick's combined state below) and the hold-to-repeat
            // timer key off this same combined signal, so all three input methods behave
            // identically regardless of which one (or which mix) is actually in use.
            bool upHeld = dpadUp || stickUp || physUpHeld;
            bool downHeld = dpadDown || stickDown || physDownHeld;
            bool leftHeld = dpadLeft || stickLeft || physLeftHeld;
            bool rightHeld = dpadRight || stickRight || physRightHeld;

            bool upPressed = upHeld && !prevUpHeld;
            bool downPressed = downHeld && !prevDownHeld;
            bool leftPressed = leftHeld && !prevLeftHeld;
            bool rightPressed = rightHeld && !prevRightHeld;

            bool upRepeat = AdvanceRepeat(upHeld, ref heldMsUp, ref repeatingUp);
            bool downRepeat = AdvanceRepeat(downHeld, ref heldMsDown, ref repeatingDown);
            bool leftRepeat = AdvanceRepeat(leftHeld, ref heldMsLeft, ref repeatingLeft);
            bool rightRepeat = AdvanceRepeat(rightHeld, ref heldMsRight, ref repeatingRight);

            // Recorded here - BEFORE FireDirectionalMove and the A/B/Y dispatch below run -
            // rather than at the very end of the tick, which is where this used to happen.
            // Opening a picker (A on a dropdown, Settings, etc.) calls ShowDialog, which pumps
            // its own nested message loop, and this same System.Windows.Forms.Timer keeps
            // ticking inside that nested loop. If "prevControllerButtons" was still holding
            // the state from BEFORE this press (because the assignment hadn't run yet), that
            // re-entrant tick would see the still-physically-held A button as a brand new
            // "just pressed" edge against the picker that had only just opened, and
            // immediately activate whatever tile was selected - which is exactly what made a
            // freshly opened dropdown "flash and instantly close" instead of staying open.
            // Updating these first means a re-entrant tick during that same button press sees
            // prevAButton already true and does nothing, the same way holding a key down
            // doesn't re-trigger a fresh keypress.
            prevControllerButtons = buttons;
            prevUpHeld = upHeld;
            prevDownHeld = downHeld;
            prevLeftHeld = leftHeld;
            prevRightHeld = rightHeld;

            FireDirectionalMove(upPressed || upRepeat, downPressed || downRepeat, leftPressed || leftRepeat, rightPressed || rightRepeat);

            if (keyboardVisible)
            {
                if (aButton && !prevAButton) ActivateKeyboardSelection();
                if (bButton && !prevBButton) HideVirtualKeyboard();
            }
            else if (activeConsolePicker != null)
            {
                // Checked ahead of every main-window zone: a picker is modal, so while one is
                // up it is the only thing on screen the buttons could sensibly mean anything to.
                if (aButton && !prevAButton) activeConsolePicker.ActivateSelection();
                if (bButton && !prevBButton) activeConsolePicker.CancelPicker();
                // Y jumps straight to the search row and summons the on-screen keyboard for it,
                // which is the shortcut printed on the row itself.
                if (yButton && !prevYButton) activeConsolePicker.BeginTyping();
            }
            else if (consoleDropdownOpen)
            {
                // Checked before consoleTopBarActive: while the list is open, B has to mean
                // "close this list" rather than "leave the whole top bar".
                if (aButton && !prevAButton) CloseConsoleDropdown(true);
                if (bButton && !prevBButton) CloseConsoleDropdown(false);
            }
            else if (consoleTopBarActive)
            {
                if (aButton && !prevAButton) ActivateConsoleTopBarSelection();
                if (bButton && !prevBButton) ExitConsoleTopBar();
            }
            else if (listResizeModeActive)
            {
                if ((aButton && !prevAButton) || (bButton && !prevBButton)) OnToggleListResizeModeClicked(this, EventArgs.Empty);
            }
            else if (consoleSidebarFocused)
            {
                if (aButton && !prevAButton) ActivateConsoleSidebarSelection();
                // B backs out one level - to the tiles - rather than straight out of Console
                // Mode, matching what B does everywhere else in this app.
                if (bButton && !prevBButton) LeaveConsoleSidebar();
            }
            else
            {
                if (aButton && !prevAButton) ActivateConsoleSelection();
                // Fix: this used to exit Console Mode entirely on B, which meant mashing B to
                // back out of a few levels of navigation (sidebar -> tiles -> here) could
                // accidentally flip all the way back to Desktop Mode with one extra press.
                // The tile grid is the top of Console Mode's own navigation stack - there's
                // nowhere further back to go within Console Mode - so B here is simply a
                // no-op now. Leaving Console Mode is still reachable, just only as a
                // deliberate action via Settings -> Switch To Desktop Mode, the same as
                // toggling it off ever was in Desktop Mode's own Settings dialog.
            }
        }

        // The 5-button row (Add/Delete Server/Delete Mod/Undo/Merge) can't use ordinary
        // Anchor=Left|Right the way a single control can, because that only stretches ONE
        // control to fill its parent - it doesn't know how to share the extra width across
        // several sibling buttons in the same row. So this recomputes all 5 positions/widths
        // by hand every time the window resizes, splitting the available width between them
        // by how wide each button's OWN label actually measures rather than splitting it
        // evenly - an even split is what caused "Delete Se..." to render truncated at the
        // window's default width: "Delete Server" is longer than "Add Server"/"Delete Mod"/
        // "Undo" but was getting the exact same share of the row as they were.
        private void LayoutActionButtonRow()
        {
            if (btnAddServerFolder == null || btnDeleteServerFolder == null || btnDeleteSelectedPak == null ||
                btnUndoLastAction == null || btnMergeServerMods == null) return;

            const int leftMargin = 15;
            const int rightMargin = 15;
            const int gap = 6;
            const int rowHeight = 28;
            const int minButtonWidth = 70;
            const int perButtonPadding = 18;
            // Read the row's CURRENT vertical position instead of hardcoding it - dragging the
            // mod list resize button (SetupListResizeButton) also moves this row up/down, and this
            // method must never fight that by snapping it back to a fixed Y on every resize.
            int rowY = btnAddServerFolder.Top;

            int totalWidth = ClientSize.Width - leftMargin - rightMargin;
            if (totalWidth < 320) totalWidth = 320;

            Button[] buttons = { btnAddServerFolder, btnDeleteServerFolder, btnDeleteSelectedPak, btnUndoLastAction, btnMergeServerMods };
            int totalGap = gap * (buttons.Length - 1);
            int usableWidth = totalWidth - totalGap;

            float[] weights = new float[buttons.Length];
            float totalWeight = 0f;
            for (int i = 0; i < buttons.Length; i++)
            {
                weights[i] = TextRenderer.MeasureText(buttons[i].Text, buttons[i].Font).Width + perButtonPadding;
                totalWeight += weights[i];
            }

            // Natural-width-first: give every button at least the width its OWN label needs
            // before handing out any leftover space proportionally. Splitting purely by
            // proportion (the old approach) could still shave a button's share a pixel or two
            // under what its text actually measured - fine for short labels like "Undo", but
            // enough to clip "Delete Server" since its natural share left almost no margin.
            int[] widths = new int[buttons.Length];
            int[] natural = new int[buttons.Length];
            int naturalTotal = 0;
            for (int i = 0; i < buttons.Length; i++)
            {
                natural[i] = Math.Max(minButtonWidth, (int)Math.Ceiling(weights[i]));
                naturalTotal += natural[i];
            }

            int assigned = 0;
            if (naturalTotal <= usableWidth)
            {
                // Enough room for every label to render in full - start from natural widths,
                // then distribute the leftover space proportionally so the row still stretches
                // to fill the window instead of leaving a gap on the right.
                int leftover = usableWidth - naturalTotal;
                for (int i = 0; i < buttons.Length; i++)
                {
                    int extra = (int)(leftover * (weights[i] / totalWeight));
                    widths[i] = natural[i] + extra;
                    assigned += widths[i];
                }
            }
            else
            {
                // Window is narrower than the row actually needs (e.g. dragged in toward
                // MinimumSize) - fall back to a proportional squeeze so buttons never overlap.
                // EnsureActionRowMinimumWidth keeps this branch from ever running at the app's
                // default/minimum size, so in practice this only bites mid-drag.
                for (int i = 0; i < buttons.Length; i++)
                {
                    widths[i] = Math.Max(minButtonWidth, (int)(usableWidth * (weights[i] / totalWeight)));
                    assigned += widths[i];
                }
            }
            // Rounding can leave a few pixels over/under the available width - folding that
            // remainder into the last button keeps the row's total width exact instead of
            // drifting past the right margin or leaving a gap there.
            widths[widths.Length - 1] = Math.Max(minButtonWidth, widths[widths.Length - 1] + (usableWidth - assigned));

            int x = leftMargin;
            for (int i = 0; i < buttons.Length; i++)
            {
                buttons[i].Location = new Point(x, rowY);
                buttons[i].Size = new Size(widths[i], rowHeight);
                x += widths[i] + gap;
            }
        }

        private void UpdateOpenEngineIniButtonText()
        {
            string editor = (cboEditorSelector.SelectedItem != null) ? cboEditorSelector.SelectedItem.ToString() : "Windows Notepad";
            btnOpenEngineIni.Text = "Open Engine.ini in " + editor;
        }

        private void AttachSearchIcon(TextBox textBox)
        {
            // The glass itself (circle + handle) is drawn slightly off-center within its own
            // 16x16 canvas - the handle only extends the shape to the bottom-right, so shifting
            // the drawing origin by half a pixel that direction balances the visible shape
            // inside its square rather than the shape looking pulled toward the top-left.
            PictureBox iconBox = new PictureBox
            {
                Size = new Size(16, 16),
                Cursor = Cursors.IBeam,
                BackColor = Color.Transparent
            };

            iconBox.Paint += delegate(object s, PaintEventArgs pe)
            {
                pe.Graphics.SmoothingMode = System.Drawing.Drawing2D.SmoothingMode.AntiAlias;
                Color color = (cboThemeSelector.SelectedItem != null && cboThemeSelector.SelectedItem.ToString() == "Light Mode") 
                    ? Color.Gray 
                    : AccentOrange;

                using (Pen pen = new Pen(color, 1.8f))
                {
                    pe.Graphics.DrawEllipse(pen, 0.5f, 0.5f, 8, 8);
                    pe.Graphics.DrawLine(pen, 7.5f, 7.5f, 12.5f, 12.5f);
                }
            };

            iconBox.Click += delegate(object s, EventArgs e) { textBox.Focus(); };

            Panel paddingPanel = new Panel
            {
                Size = new Size(20, textBox.ClientSize.Height),
                Dock = DockStyle.Left,
                BackColor = Color.Transparent
            };
            paddingPanel.Controls.Add(iconBox);

            // Center the icon inside its little square margin area by measured size rather
            // than a hardcoded offset, so it stays centered regardless of the textbox's actual
            // rendered height (which varies with font/DPI) instead of assuming a fixed height.
            Action centerIconInPanel = delegate
            {
                iconBox.Location = new Point(
                    (paddingPanel.ClientSize.Width - iconBox.Width) / 2,
                    (paddingPanel.ClientSize.Height - iconBox.Height) / 2);
            };
            centerIconInPanel();
            paddingPanel.Resize += delegate { centerIconInPanel(); };

            textBox.Controls.Add(paddingPanel);

            SendMessage(textBox.Handle, EM_SETMARGINS, (IntPtr)EC_LEFTMARGIN, (IntPtr)(20 & 0xFFFF));
        }

        // Whenever the "On-Screen Virtual Keyboard" setting is on, focusing any wired text box
        // (by mouse, touch, or controller-driven Console Mode navigation) pops the themed
        // keyboard up targeting that box - the only way a controller-only session can type at
        // all, and a convenience for touchscreens on top of that.
        private void AttachVirtualKeyboardOnFocus(TextBox textBox)
        {
            textBox.GotFocus += delegate
            {
                // suppressKeyboardAutoShow is set while HideVirtualKeyboard is actively moving
                // focus off a textbox it just closed for - without this check, that hand-off
                // would immediately re-trigger this same handler and pop the keyboard back open.
                if (!suppressKeyboardAutoShow && chkVirtualKeyboard != null && chkVirtualKeyboard.Checked
                    && chkConsoleMode != null && chkConsoleMode.Checked)
                {
                    ShowVirtualKeyboard(textBox);
                }
            };
        }

        // --- Virtual Keyboard construction/behavior ---

        // Fix: the keyboard popup used to be a plain "new Form" that only wired up Up/Down/
        // Left/Right through its KeyDown event (with KeyPreview=true). That looked like it
        // should work, but a focused Button intercepts arrow keys earlier in the message
        // pipeline - via ProcessCmdKey/dialog-key routing - than a Form's own KeyDown/
        // KeyPreview ever sees them, so the presses silently never reached the handler at all
        // and the on-screen selector didn't move. The main window's own D-pad/arrow handling
        // (see ModManagerForm.ProcessCmdKey above) already sidesteps this the correct way: by
        // overriding ProcessCmdKey itself, which is called earlier and bubbles up from
        // whichever child control is focused. This small subclass gives the keyboard popup
        // that same, already-proven mechanism instead of relying on KeyDown/KeyPreview.
        private class VirtualKeyboardForm : Form
        {
            // Nested classes can reach the outer instance's private members directly, so this
            // just needs a reference to route the same phys*Held flags/actions
            // ControllerPollTimer_Tick already reads for the main window's own navigation.
            public ModManagerForm Host;

            protected override bool ProcessCmdKey(ref Message msg, Keys keyData)
            {
                if (Host != null)
                {
                    if (keyData == Keys.Up) { Host.physUpHeld = true; return true; }
                    if (keyData == Keys.Down) { Host.physDownHeld = true; return true; }
                    if (keyData == Keys.Left) { Host.physLeftHeld = true; return true; }
                    if (keyData == Keys.Right) { Host.physRightHeld = true; return true; }
                    if (keyData == Keys.Enter || keyData == Keys.Space) { Host.ActivateKeyboardSelection(); return true; }
                    if (keyData == Keys.Escape) { Host.HideVirtualKeyboard(); return true; }
                }
                return base.ProcessCmdKey(ref msg, keyData);
            }
        }

        // Same characters in both rows 1/2/3/4 whether Symbols mode is on or not - keeps the
        // grid shape (and therefore the selected column) identical across the toggle, so
        // switching modes never has to re-clamp keyboardSelCol.
        private static readonly string[] KeyboardLettersRows = { "1234567890", "QWERTYUIOP", "ASDFGHJKL", "ZXCVBNM" };
        private static readonly string[] KeyboardSymbolsRows = { "1234567890", "!@#$%^&*()", "-_=+;:'\"/", ",.?!/\\~" };

        private void BuildVirtualKeyboard()
        {
            frmVirtualKeyboard = new VirtualKeyboardForm
            {
                Host = this,
                FormBorderStyle = FormBorderStyle.None,
                ShowInTaskbar = false,
                StartPosition = FormStartPosition.Manual,
                Size = new Size(430, 236),
                KeyPreview = true
            };

            // A physical-keyboard equivalent of the controller D-pad/A/B handling in
            // ControllerPollTimer_Tick. Up/Down/Left/Right (captured via VirtualKeyboardForm's
            // ProcessCmdKey override above, not KeyDown - see the comment on that class for
            // why) no longer move the selection directly on every press - they just mark the
            // direction physically held (physUpHeld etc., cleared by the KeyUp handler right
            // below), and ControllerPollTimer_Tick performs the actual move(s) - both the
            // immediate first one and any hold-to-repeat ones - the same way it does for a held
            // D-pad direction, so both repeat at an identical, controlled speed instead of
            // whatever the OS's own keyboard-repeat rate happens to be. Enter/Space/Escape are
            // one-shot actions with no repeat, so ProcessCmdKey fires them directly.
            frmVirtualKeyboard.KeyUp += OnConsoleModeKeyUp;

            btnKeyboardClose = new ShinyButton
            {
                Text = "\u25BC  Close Keyboard  (B)",
                Font = new Font(FontFamily.GenericSansSerif, 9f, FontStyle.Bold),
                FlatStyle = FlatStyle.Flat
            };
            btnKeyboardClose.Click += delegate { HideVirtualKeyboard(); };
            frmVirtualKeyboard.Controls.Add(btnKeyboardClose);

            List<Button> row0 = new List<Button> { btnKeyboardClose };
            keyboardKeyRows.Add(row0);

            // Rows 1-4: letters/numbers, re-labeled in place (never rebuilt) whenever
            // Shift/Symbols toggles - see RebuildKeyboardLabels.
            for (int r = 0; r < KeyboardLettersRows.Length; r++)
            {
                List<Button> row = new List<Button>();
                for (int c = 0; c < KeyboardLettersRows[r].Length; c++)
                {
                    Button key = new Button
                    {
                        Font = new Font(FontFamily.GenericSansSerif, 9.5f, FontStyle.Bold),
                        FlatStyle = FlatStyle.Flat,
                        Tag = new int[] { r, c }
                    };
                    key.FlatAppearance.BorderSize = 1;
                    key.Click += KeyboardCharKey_Click;
                    frmVirtualKeyboard.Controls.Add(key);
                    row.Add(key);
                }
                keyboardKeyRows.Add(row);
            }

            Button btnShift = new Button { Text = "\u21E7", Font = new Font(FontFamily.GenericSansSerif, 10f, FontStyle.Bold), FlatStyle = FlatStyle.Flat };
            btnShift.FlatAppearance.BorderSize = 1;
            btnShift.Click += delegate { keyboardShiftActive = !keyboardShiftActive; RebuildKeyboardLabels(); RefreshKeyboardHighlight(); };

            Button btnSymbols = new Button { Text = "123", Font = new Font(FontFamily.GenericSansSerif, 9f, FontStyle.Bold), FlatStyle = FlatStyle.Flat };
            btnSymbols.FlatAppearance.BorderSize = 1;
            btnSymbols.Click += delegate { keyboardSymbolsActive = !keyboardSymbolsActive; RebuildKeyboardLabels(); RefreshKeyboardHighlight(); };

            Button btnSpace = new Button { Text = "Space", Font = new Font(FontFamily.GenericSansSerif, 9f, FontStyle.Regular), FlatStyle = FlatStyle.Flat };
            btnSpace.FlatAppearance.BorderSize = 1;
            btnSpace.Click += delegate { InsertTextToTarget(" "); };

            Button btnBackspace = new Button { Text = "\u232B", Font = new Font(FontFamily.GenericSansSerif, 10f, FontStyle.Bold), FlatStyle = FlatStyle.Flat };
            btnBackspace.FlatAppearance.BorderSize = 1;
            btnBackspace.Click += delegate { BackspaceTarget(); };

            Button btnEnter = new Button { Text = "Enter \u23CE", Font = new Font(FontFamily.GenericSansSerif, 9f, FontStyle.Bold), FlatStyle = FlatStyle.Flat };
            btnEnter.FlatAppearance.BorderSize = 1;
            btnEnter.Click += delegate
            {
                if (keyboardTargetTextBox != null && keyboardTargetTextBox.Multiline) InsertTextToTarget("\r\n");
                else HideVirtualKeyboard();
            };

            List<Button> lastRow = new List<Button> { btnShift, btnSymbols, btnSpace, btnBackspace, btnEnter };
            foreach (Button b in lastRow) frmVirtualKeyboard.Controls.Add(b);
            keyboardKeyRows.Add(lastRow);

            frmVirtualKeyboard.Resize += delegate { LayoutVirtualKeyboardKeys(); };

            RebuildKeyboardLabels();
            LayoutVirtualKeyboardKeys();
        }

        // Rows are laid out on a simple grid: every row gets an equal share of the panel's
        // width, split evenly among that row's own keys - except the last row, where Space
        // is deliberately given the lion's share (matches every real on-screen keyboard).
        private void LayoutVirtualKeyboardKeys()
        {
            if (frmVirtualKeyboard == null || keyboardKeyRows.Count == 0) return;

            const int margin = 6;
            const int gap = 4;
            int width = frmVirtualKeyboard.ClientSize.Width - margin * 2;
            int rowCount = keyboardKeyRows.Count;
            int rowHeight = (frmVirtualKeyboard.ClientSize.Height - margin * 2 - gap * (rowCount - 1)) / rowCount;

            int y = margin;
            for (int r = 0; r < keyboardKeyRows.Count; r++)
            {
                List<Button> row = keyboardKeyRows[r];

                if (r == 0)
                {
                    row[0].Location = new Point(margin, y);
                    row[0].Size = new Size(width, rowHeight);
                }
                else if (r == keyboardKeyRows.Count - 1)
                {
                    // Shift, 123/ABC, Space (wide), Backspace, Enter
                    int narrowWidth = (int)(width * 0.14);
                    int wideWidth = width - narrowWidth * 4 - gap * 4;
                    int x = margin;
                    int[] widths = { narrowWidth, narrowWidth, wideWidth, narrowWidth, narrowWidth };
                    for (int c = 0; c < row.Count; c++)
                    {
                        row[c].Location = new Point(x, y);
                        row[c].Size = new Size(widths[c], rowHeight);
                        x += widths[c] + gap;
                    }
                }
                else
                {
                    int keyWidth = (width - gap * (row.Count - 1)) / row.Count;
                    int x = margin;
                    for (int c = 0; c < row.Count; c++)
                    {
                        row[c].Location = new Point(x, y);
                        row[c].Size = new Size(keyWidth, rowHeight);
                        x += keyWidth + gap;
                    }
                }

                y += rowHeight + gap;
            }
        }

        // Re-applies every character key's displayed text from the active layout/shift state -
        // called on build and whenever Shift or the 123/ABC toggle changes. The keys
        // themselves are never recreated, just relabeled.
        private void RebuildKeyboardLabels()
        {
            string[] activeRows = keyboardSymbolsActive ? KeyboardSymbolsRows : KeyboardLettersRows;

            for (int r = 1; r <= KeyboardLettersRows.Length; r++)
            {
                List<Button> row = keyboardKeyRows[r];
                string sourceRow = activeRows[r - 1];
                for (int c = 0; c < row.Count; c++)
                {
                    char ch = sourceRow[c];
                    bool isLetter = !keyboardSymbolsActive && char.IsLetter(ch);
                    row[c].Text = isLetter
                        ? (keyboardShiftActive ? char.ToUpperInvariant(ch).ToString() : char.ToLowerInvariant(ch).ToString())
                        : ch.ToString();
                }
            }
        }

        private void KeyboardCharKey_Click(object sender, EventArgs e)
        {
            Button key = sender as Button;
            if (key == null) return;
            InsertTextToTarget(key.Text);
        }

        // Inserts at the caret (replacing any current selection) rather than always appending,
        // so backspacing/retyping mid-string works the way it would with a real keyboard.
        private void InsertTextToTarget(string text)
        {
            if (keyboardTargetTextBox == null || keyboardTargetTextBox.IsDisposed) return;

            TextBox target = keyboardTargetTextBox;
            int caret = target.SelectionStart;
            target.Text = target.Text.Remove(caret, target.SelectionLength).Insert(caret, text);
            target.SelectionStart = caret + text.Length;
            target.SelectionLength = 0;
            target.Focus();
        }

        private void BackspaceTarget()
        {
            if (keyboardTargetTextBox == null || keyboardTargetTextBox.IsDisposed) return;

            TextBox target = keyboardTargetTextBox;
            if (target.SelectionLength > 0)
            {
                int caret = target.SelectionStart;
                target.Text = target.Text.Remove(caret, target.SelectionLength);
                target.SelectionStart = caret;
            }
            else if (target.SelectionStart > 0)
            {
                int caret = target.SelectionStart - 1;
                target.Text = target.Text.Remove(caret, 1);
                target.SelectionStart = caret;
            }
            target.Focus();
        }

        // Positions the keyboard just under whichever control it's targeting (clamped to the
        // owning screen's working area so it can never be dragged/opened off-screen), themes
        // it to match the current app theme, and shows it as a non-modal window OWNED by
        // whichever Form the target lives on - Owner is what lets it float above a modal
        // ShowThemedInputBox/ShowSettingsDialog-style dialog without blocking it, and what
        // makes it close itself automatically if that dialog closes first.
        private void ShowVirtualKeyboard(TextBox target)
        {
            if (frmVirtualKeyboard == null || target == null || target.IsDisposed) return;

            // The on-screen keyboard only exists to make text fields reachable without a
            // physical keyboard, which is only ever true in Console Mode (controller
            // navigation). In desktop mode it has no reason to exist - and letting it pop up
            // there was actively harmful: WinForms auto-focuses the first tab-order control
            // (txtGamePath, the Game Paks Directory field) the instant the main window loads,
            // which used to fire this same codepath and plant the keyboard right over the
            // window's own titlebar on launch, blocking the minimize/maximize/X buttons before
            // the user had touched anything. Gating the whole popup on Console Mode fixes that
            // launch-time bug and matches the feature as designed: no virtual keyboard outside
            // Console Mode, full stop.
            if (chkConsoleMode == null || !chkConsoleMode.Checked) return;

            keyboardTargetTextBox = target;
            keyboardSelRow = 0;
            keyboardSelCol = 0;

            Form owner = target.FindForm();
            if (!ReferenceEquals(frmVirtualKeyboard.Owner, owner))
            {
                frmVirtualKeyboard.Owner = owner;
            }

            // WinForms automatically closes (not just hides) every Form it owns when the owner
            // itself closes - fine for the main window, since that's app shutdown anyway, but
            // it would silently destroy this reused keyboard Form the first time it was shown
            // from a short-lived dialog like ShowThemedInputBox. Detaching Owner (and hiding)
            // just before that dialog closes keeps the keyboard alive for next time instead.
            if (owner != null && !ReferenceEquals(owner, this))
            {
                FormClosingEventHandler detach = null;
                detach = delegate
                {
                    if (frmVirtualKeyboard != null)
                    {
                        frmVirtualKeyboard.Owner = null;
                        frmVirtualKeyboard.Hide();
                    }
                    owner.FormClosing -= detach;
                };
                owner.FormClosing += detach;
            }

            ThemeVirtualKeyboard();

            Point screenAnchor = target.PointToScreen(new Point(0, target.Height + 4));
            Rectangle workArea = Screen.FromControl(target).WorkingArea;
            int x = Math.Max(workArea.Left, Math.Min(screenAnchor.X, workArea.Right - frmVirtualKeyboard.Width));
            int y = screenAnchor.Y;
            if (y + frmVirtualKeyboard.Height > workArea.Bottom)
            {
                // Not enough room below the target - show it above instead.
                y = target.PointToScreen(Point.Empty).Y - frmVirtualKeyboard.Height - 4;
            }
            frmVirtualKeyboard.Location = new Point(x, Math.Max(workArea.Top, y));

            RefreshKeyboardHighlight();

            if (!frmVirtualKeyboard.Visible)
            {
                frmVirtualKeyboard.Show(owner);
            }
            else
            {
                frmVirtualKeyboard.BringToFront();
            }

            // Fix: neither Show() nor BringToFront() reliably hands this borderless, no-caption
            // popup real Windows input focus - Show() usually does on a fresh open, but
            // BringToFront() (the path used when the keyboard is already open and the user just
            // moved to a different field) only reorders z-order and leaves focus wherever it
            // already was, which is the textbox that was just focused via
            // AttachVirtualKeyboardOnFocus's GotFocus handler. With no real mouse click ever
            // happening to naturally activate this window (the whole point of the keyboard is
            // controller/touch-only input), that textbox - not this Form - kept real OS focus.
            // Every physical/emulated arrow-key or Enter press then landed on whatever was
            // actually focused instead of on frmVirtualKeyboard's own KeyDown handler above:
            // Left/Right got eaten by the textbox's native caret movement (so they looked like
            // they "did nothing" to the keyboard), while Up/Down and Enter fell through to
            // whatever the underlying window did with them - Console Mode's top-bar/tile
            // navigation on the main form, moving between FIELDS instead of between KEYS, and
            // making the on-screen Close button unreachable via Enter. Explicitly activating
            // and focusing the keyboard Form every time it's shown or re-targeted guarantees
            // every subsequent key press actually reaches its own grid navigation instead.
            frmVirtualKeyboard.Activate();
            frmVirtualKeyboard.Focus();

            // Controller D-pad navigation over the keyboard's own keys is driven by the same
            // poll timer Console Mode uses - see ControllerPollTimer_Tick, which now checks
            // "is the keyboard visible" independently of whether Console Mode itself is on, so
            // this works even for a controller user who never turned Console Mode on at all.
            controllerPollTimer.Start();
        }

        private void HideVirtualKeyboard()
        {
            if (frmVirtualKeyboard == null) return;

            // Fix: this used to just Hide() the popup and clear keyboardTargetTextBox without
            // ever moving real Windows focus off the textbox itself. That left two things
            // broken: (1) the textbox was still the focused control, so if focus ever came
            // back to this window from elsewhere (e.g. alt-tabbing back in), its GotFocus
            // handler (AttachVirtualKeyboardOnFocus) fired again and popped the keyboard right
            // back open even though the user had just closed it; and (2) with the textbox
            // still focused, arrow keys kept moving its text caret instead of reaching Console
            // Mode's D-pad/keyboard tile navigation. suppressKeyboardAutoShow (previously
            // declared but never actually read anywhere) now guards the GotFocus handler while
            // we shift focus away below, so that hand-off can't immediately reopen the keyboard.
            suppressKeyboardAutoShow = true;
            try
            {
                TextBox target = keyboardTargetTextBox;

                // The Game Paks Directory field is the one text box in the app whose value is
                // meant to be durable (persisted to ConfigFileName - see PersistConfigPath),
                // and it's the one field Console Mode users can only ever edit through this
                // on-screen keyboard (see OpenConsolePathPicker's "Type The Path" option). Only
                // OnBrowsePathClicked's folder-browse flow was actually calling
                // PersistConfigPath, so a path typed here looked like it "took" (the text box
                // updates immediately) but silently reverted to whatever was last saved the
                // next time the app launched. Persisting here, right as the keyboard that just
                // edited it closes, covers that path the same way txtGamePath's own Leave
                // handler (see its creation) covers a real physical keyboard doing the typing.
                if (ReferenceEquals(target, txtGamePath) && txtGamePath != null)
                {
                    PersistConfigPath(txtGamePath.Text.Trim());
                }

                // Fix: the keyboard is a borderless popup that takes real foreground focus
                // while it's open (see the Activate/Focus calls in ShowVirtualKeyboard). Just
                // calling Hide() on the foreground window leaves Windows to pick the next
                // window in Z-order itself, and that is frequently NOT this app - it's
                // whatever happens to be behind it, typically the PowerShell/terminal window
                // this was launched from if it was never minimized. Explicitly activating the
                // owner BEFORE hiding hands the foreground back to the app's own window, so
                // closing the keyboard can't yank another window in front.
                Form keyboardOwner = frmVirtualKeyboard.Owner;
                if (keyboardOwner == null || keyboardOwner.IsDisposed) keyboardOwner = this;
                if (!keyboardOwner.IsDisposed && keyboardOwner.Visible)
                {
                    keyboardOwner.Activate();
                }

                frmVirtualKeyboard.Hide();
                keyboardTargetTextBox = null;

                // Activated a second time after the Hide as well: on some Windows builds the
                // pre-hide activation is undone by the hide itself, and this second call is a
                // no-op when it isn't.
                if (!keyboardOwner.IsDisposed && keyboardOwner.Visible)
                {
                    keyboardOwner.Activate();
                }

                if (target != null && !target.IsDisposed && target.Focused)
                {
                    if (pnlConsoleTiles != null && pnlConsoleTiles.Visible)
                    {
                        pnlConsoleTiles.Focus();
                    }
                    else
                    {
                        // Not in Console Mode (or the tile panel can't take focus right now) -
                        // clearing ActiveControl hands focus back to the form itself instead of
                        // leaving it stuck in the textbox.
                        this.ActiveControl = null;
                    }
                }
            }
            finally
            {
                suppressKeyboardAutoShow = false;
            }

            if ((chkConsoleMode == null || !chkConsoleMode.Checked) && !consoleTopBarActive)
            {
                controllerPollTimer.Stop();
            }
        }

        private void MoveKeyboardSelection(int dRow, int dCol)
        {
            if (keyboardKeyRows.Count == 0) return;

            if (dRow != 0)
            {
                int newRow = Math.Max(0, Math.Min(keyboardKeyRows.Count - 1, keyboardSelRow + dRow));
                if (newRow != keyboardSelRow)
                {
                    // Fix: this used to just clamp the same column INDEX into the new row
                    // (Math.Min(keyboardSelCol, newRow.Count - 1)). That only lines up by
                    // coincidence - the rows have different key counts (10/10/9/7), and the
                    // last row's five keys are deliberately very unevenly sized (Space is much
                    // wider than Shift/123/Backspace/Enter), so "same index" often lands on a
                    // key nowhere near where the old one was on screen. Real keyboards (and
                    // the D-pad speed the user already liked) work by physical position, not
                    // index, so find whichever key in the new row is horizontally closest -
                    // by actual pixel center, using the real Locations/Sizes Layout
                    // VirtualKeyboardKeys already assigned - to the key we're leaving.
                    List<Button> fromRow = keyboardKeyRows[keyboardSelRow];
                    int fromIndex = Math.Max(0, Math.Min(fromRow.Count - 1, keyboardSelCol));
                    int fromCenterX = fromRow[fromIndex].Left + fromRow[fromIndex].Width / 2;

                    List<Button> toRow = keyboardKeyRows[newRow];
                    int bestCol = 0;
                    int bestDist = int.MaxValue;
                    for (int c = 0; c < toRow.Count; c++)
                    {
                        int centerX = toRow[c].Left + toRow[c].Width / 2;
                        int dist = Math.Abs(centerX - fromCenterX);
                        if (dist < bestDist)
                        {
                            bestDist = dist;
                            bestCol = c;
                        }
                    }

                    keyboardSelRow = newRow;
                    keyboardSelCol = bestCol;
                }
            }
            if (dCol != 0)
            {
                List<Button> row = keyboardKeyRows[keyboardSelRow];
                keyboardSelCol = Math.Max(0, Math.Min(row.Count - 1, keyboardSelCol + dCol));
            }

            RefreshKeyboardHighlight();
        }

        private void ActivateKeyboardSelection()
        {
            if (keyboardSelRow < 0 || keyboardSelRow >= keyboardKeyRows.Count) return;
            List<Button> row = keyboardKeyRows[keyboardSelRow];
            if (keyboardSelCol < 0 || keyboardSelCol >= row.Count) return;
            row[keyboardSelCol].PerformClick();
        }

        private void RefreshKeyboardHighlight()
        {
            if (frmVirtualKeyboard == null) return;
            ThemeColors t = GetThemeColors(CurrentThemeName());

            for (int r = 0; r < keyboardKeyRows.Count; r++)
            {
                List<Button> row = keyboardKeyRows[r];
                for (int c = 0; c < row.Count; c++)
                {
                    bool selected = (r == keyboardSelRow && c == keyboardSelCol);
                    row[c].BackColor = selected ? t.AccentColor : t.ButtonBg;
                    row[c].ForeColor = selected ? Color.White : t.ButtonFg;
                    // These are plain flat Buttons, so with no explicit border color they fall
                    // back to a system default that is nearly invisible against Light Mode's
                    // pale key faces - the keyboard looked like one undivided gray slab. A
                    // thicker border on the selected key also keeps the cursor findable if the
                    // accent fill alone isn't obvious at a glance.
                    row[c].FlatAppearance.BorderColor = t.IsLightBase ? Color.FromArgb(120, 124, 130) : Color.FromArgb(70, 70, 78);
                    row[c].FlatAppearance.BorderSize = selected ? 2 : 1;
                }
            }

            // Shift/Symbols show their toggled-on state persistently (not just while
            // highlighted), same convention as the Resize-mode tile elsewhere in the app.
            Button shiftBtn = keyboardKeyRows[keyboardKeyRows.Count - 1][0];
            Button symbolsBtn = keyboardKeyRows[keyboardKeyRows.Count - 1][1];
            if (keyboardShiftActive && !(keyboardSelRow == keyboardKeyRows.Count - 1 && keyboardSelCol == 0)) shiftBtn.BackColor = t.AccentColor;
            if (keyboardSymbolsActive && !(keyboardSelRow == keyboardKeyRows.Count - 1 && keyboardSelCol == 1)) symbolsBtn.BackColor = t.AccentColor;
            symbolsBtn.Text = keyboardSymbolsActive ? "ABC" : "123";
        }

        private void ThemeVirtualKeyboard()
        {
            if (frmVirtualKeyboard == null) return;
            ThemeColors t = GetThemeColors(CurrentThemeName());

            frmVirtualKeyboard.BackColor = t.WindowBg;
            btnKeyboardClose.BackColor = t.AccentColor;
            btnKeyboardClose.ForeColor = Color.White;
            RefreshKeyboardHighlight();
        }

        private class ThemeColors
        {
            public Color WindowBg;
            public Color ControlBg;
            public Color TextColor;
            public Color HeaderColor;
            public Color ButtonBg;
            public Color ButtonFg;
            public Color AccentColor;
            public bool IsLightBase;
            public bool UseBlackBorder;
            public bool UseDarkScrollbar;
            public bool DarkTitleBar;
            public Color TitleBarColor;
            public Color TitleBarTextColor;
        }

        private string CurrentThemeName()
        {
            return cboThemeSelector.SelectedItem != null ? cboThemeSelector.SelectedItem.ToString() : "Dark Mode";
        }

        private enum SemanticColorRole { Accent, Danger, Success, Info }

        // Okabe-Ito-derived colorblind-safe palette. colorBlindMode == "Off" leaves every
        // color exactly as the theme defined it; each other mode remaps the app's
        // meaning-carrying colors (red = delete/danger, green = add/launch/success, blue =
        // undo/info, plus the general accent) to hues that stay distinguishable under that
        // specific color vision deficiency, rather than leaning on red vs. green - the
        // single hardest pair for the two most common types (Protanopia/Deuteranopia).
        private Color AdjustForColorBlindness(Color original, SemanticColorRole role)
        {
            switch (colorBlindMode)
            {
                case "Protanopia":
                    switch (role)
                    {
                        case SemanticColorRole.Danger: return Color.FromArgb(213, 94, 0);    // vermillion
                        case SemanticColorRole.Success: return Color.FromArgb(0, 114, 178);  // blue
                        case SemanticColorRole.Accent: return Color.FromArgb(86, 180, 233);  // sky blue
                        default: return Color.FromArgb(0, 114, 178);
                    }
                case "Deuteranopia":
                    switch (role)
                    {
                        case SemanticColorRole.Danger: return Color.FromArgb(213, 94, 0);    // vermillion
                        case SemanticColorRole.Success: return Color.FromArgb(0, 114, 178);  // blue
                        case SemanticColorRole.Accent: return Color.FromArgb(230, 159, 0);   // orange
                        default: return Color.FromArgb(0, 114, 178);
                    }
                case "Tritanopia":
                    switch (role)
                    {
                        case SemanticColorRole.Danger: return Color.FromArgb(213, 94, 0);    // vermillion (reds still read fine here)
                        case SemanticColorRole.Success: return Color.FromArgb(0, 158, 115);  // bluish green
                        case SemanticColorRole.Accent: return Color.FromArgb(204, 121, 167); // reddish purple
                        default: return Color.FromArgb(0, 158, 115);
                    }
                default:
                    return original;
            }
        }

        private ThemeColors GetThemeColors(string themeName)
        {
            ThemeColors t = GetBaseThemeColors(themeName);

            // The Accent color carries one specific, hand-tuned meaning ("this is the
            // interactive highlight"), so every theme's accent lands on the exact same
            // tested Okabe-Ito substitution below rather than just being nudged away from
            // whatever hue that particular theme happened to pick.
            t.AccentColor = AdjustForColorBlindness(t.AccentColor, SemanticColorRole.Accent);

            // Everything else that carries a theme's own brand hue - window/control
            // backgrounds, header text, plain button backgrounds, and the title bar -
            // previously stayed exactly as the theme defined them no matter which Colorblind
            // Mode was selected, so switching the mode only ever changed a handful of action
            // buttons and left the rest of the window (which is most of what's actually on
            // screen) untouched. Running them through the generic hue-bucket remapper below
            // closes that gap: any hue that falls in a band that collides under the selected
            // deficiency gets rotated to a safe one, at the exact same saturation and
            // lightness, so the fix reads as "this hue moved" rather than "everything went
            // gray."
            t.WindowBg = AdjustHueForColorBlindness(t.WindowBg);
            t.ControlBg = AdjustHueForColorBlindness(t.ControlBg);
            t.HeaderColor = AdjustHueForColorBlindness(t.HeaderColor);
            t.ButtonBg = AdjustHueForColorBlindness(t.ButtonBg);
            t.TitleBarColor = AdjustHueForColorBlindness(t.TitleBarColor);
            return t;
        }

        // General-purpose companion to AdjustForColorBlindness above: that one remaps a FIXED
        // handful of named roles (Accent/Danger/Success/Info) to one specific tested hue each,
        // regardless of the theme. This one instead looks at whatever hue a color already has
        // and only rotates it if that hue sits in a band that's genuinely hard to tell apart
        // from another band under the selected deficiency - so it can be applied blindly to
        // every theme color (backgrounds, header text, title bars, plain buttons) without
        // needing a hand-picked target for each one individually.
        private Color AdjustHueForColorBlindness(Color c)
        {
            if (colorBlindMode == "Off") return c;
